hasta
(‘hand’)
------------------------------------------
Though the word means ‘hand’ in general, it is used in a more technical sense also. It is the same as cubit, the length between the elbow and the end of the middle finger. It is 24 aṅgulas or 18 inches. This measurement is often used to specify the dimensions of a building, a tank, an embankment and so on.
When a होउसे has to be built, the architect takes the owner’s or his wife’s or his eldest son’s cubit as the basic standard of length.
The word is sometimes used in place of the word ‘mudrā’ (hand-pose) as, for instance, in ‘abhayahasta’ and ‘varadahasta’.

Hastināpura
(‘city of Hastin’)
------------------------------------------
Hastināpura or Hastināvatī has been known to all those familiar with the epic, the Mahābhārata, as the capital city of the कुरु race of kings—the Kauravas first, and then, of the Pāṇḍavas.
King Hastin was an ancestor of the Kauravas and the Pāṇḍavas. He was the son of Bṛhatkṣattra, a king of the चन्द्रवṁश or Lunar race. He built this city during his reign and hence it came to be known as ‘Hastināpura’ or ‘Hastinā-vatī’. During the reign of Nicaknu, a descendant of the Pāṇḍavas, the city is said to have been devastated by floods in the गङ्गा, forcing him to shift his capital to Kauśāmbi (vide Viṣṇupurāṇa 4.21).
The site of हस्तिनापुर has been located at a place, 90 kms. (56 miles) to the north-east of Delhi. The excavation done by the Archaeological Survey of India in 1949 revealed that the earliest inhabitants there, used ochre-coloured pottery and copper vessels. The city may have been abandoned due to a rise in the level of the river गङ्गा.
There are reasons to believe that the city was reoccupied after some time. Relics assigned to this period include sun-dried brick-walls, copper and iron utensils, clay figurines and die-stamped coins.
It might have been abandoned again around 300 B. C. and reoccupied a second time after a lapse of about a hundred years.

Hasta-sāmudrika-śāstra
(‘the science of [prognostication by studying] the lines in the palm of the hand’)
------------------------------------------
The desire to know the future has been a natural instinct with the human beings. This has led to the discovery or invention of many new fields of knowledge. One of them is पल्मिस्त्र्य्, called ‘Hastasāmudrikaśāstra’ by the Hindu scriptures.
It is said that Samudrarāja (the king of the ocean) once studied the various marks on the body of Lord विष्णु who was in योगनिद्रा (deep meditation) and explained their specialities to his eager disciples. That is why this science came to be known as ‘Sāmudrikaśāstra’.
According to an ancient tradition, प्रह्लाद (the great child-devotee of Lord विष्णु) was the original teacher of this science.
Some of the ancient treatises on this science are: Gargasaṁhitā, Garuḍa-purāṇa, Sāmudrikabhoja, Parāśara-sāmudrikaśāstra and Hastasañjīvanī.
The Sāmudrikaśāstra has branched off into three wings. They are: हस्त-sāmudrika, Aṅgasāmudrika and स्त्री-sāmudrika.
Whereas Aṅgasāmudrika deals with the study of the characteristics of all the limbs (= aṅgas) of the body, the हस्त-sāmudrika concerns itself only with the study of the हस्त, the hand or the palm. The last branch deals exclusively with the characteristic signs on the bodies of women.
Anyone who wants to practise हस्त-sāmudrikaśāstra, should be well-conversant with ज्यौतिष or अस्त्रोलोग्य् also. Any prognostication has to depend on a study of the palms as also the horoscopes.
While studying the hand, the palmist has to see the right hand of men and the left hand of women. The palms of children can be examined only if they are past fourteen years of age.
The following are the factors which have to be studied carefully with regard to the hand and the palm before drawing any conclusions:
Length of fingers as also the position of the lines at the finger-joints; the various mounts or bulged portions, generally at the roots of the fingers; lines on the palms; various signs in the shape of शङ्ख (conch), चक्र (discus), triangle, fish, bow, lotus, star and so on.
Experts in this field opine that apart from studying at least five thousand hands, the palmist should also lead a good life, practise योग and acquire some basic knowledge of Hindu अस्त्रोलोग्य् before prognostication based on the study of the hands and the palms.

Hastāmalaka
(‘[one who knows a thing thoroughly like knowing] a myrobalan placed in the hand’)
------------------------------------------
When शङ्कर (A.

-820) the great teacher of the renaissance of Vedic religion and philosophy, came to a small town, Śrībali by name, in Karnataka, he heard of a ‘dull’ boy who appeared to be deaf and dumb too. He was the son of प्रभाकर, a well-known ब्राह्मण of that place. When प्रभाकर met शङ्कर and poured out his heart about his ‘misfortune,’ शङ्कर questioned the boy, ‘Who are you my boy? Why are you behaving like a dullard?’
The boy at once blurted out for the first time in his life, ‘I am not a jaḍa (inert) but the jaḍa springs into action by my presence!’
He is said to have replied in fourteen verses which are full of Vedāntic (advaitic) wisdom. This has now come to be known as the Hastāmalakastotra.
Śaṅkara immediately recognised him as a highly evolved सोउल् and asked प्रभाकर to gift the boy to him. This boy was named ‘Hastāmalaka’ since he knew his real nature as the आत्मन् as clearly as knowing a myrobalan fruit placed in the palm of one’s hand (hasta = palm, आमलक = myrobalan) and became the third of the four chief disciples of शङ्कर. He later on assumed charge as the first pontiff of गोवर्धन मठ at पुरी (in Orissa).
See also ŚAṄKARĀCĀRYA.
